V38_ABSTRACT: Prompt Cartography: Interactive Map Design with LLMs is a practical, research-informed guide to directing large language models and AI agents to design modern interactive maps across web, mobile, and emerging natural-language GIS platforms. It highlights how cartographic principles such as design, ethics, and spatial communication remain vital despite technological shifts and emphasizes the importance of understanding coding and data literacy to responsibly integrate AI tools like LLMs into workflows. It reframes cartographers as media directors who articulate intent, ethics, and design decisions in structured natural language that LLMs then execute, critique, and iterate at scale. Features Demonstrates how to design complete prompt-to-map pipelines for web cartography, from semantic data discovery and cleaning through visual form, symbology, interactivity, and publication decisions. Connects classic cartographic principles like visual hierarchy, visual literacy, thematic map types, color, and typography rules directly to prompt structures and reusable natural-language patterns. Shows how to manage LLM defaults, guard against hallucinations, and encode ethical constraints around provenance, privacy, bias, and civic accountability directly into prompts and agent workflows. Explains techniques for orchestrating multiple LLM agents, such as data finders, critics, visualizers, and publishers, into robust map design pipelines that make expert judgment visible instead of implicit. Provides end-to-end seminar-style case studies, from exploratory analysis to civic-facing web maps, that expose real missteps, revisions, and decision points in prompt cartography practice. Includes conceptual exercises, applied labs, and companion website materials with evolving prompt templates, schemas, and implementation examples for a variety of web mapping platforms. Acts as a stand-alone text, but it can also serve as a bridge for readers of Web Cartography to bring their existing cartographic expertise into the era of AI-assisted, prompt-driven interactive mapping. This book is aimed at undergraduate and graduate students in GIS, cartography, geography, and related fields, as well as working professionals who need to incorporate LLMs and natural-language workflows into their map design practice without surrendering aesthetic quality, ethical responsibility, or authorial judgment and control.

title: Automating Cyber Risk Assessment With Public LLMs: An Expert-Validated Framework and Comparative Analysis

V38_RECOVERED_TITLE: Automating Cyber Risk Assessment With Public LLMs: An Expert-Validated Framework and Comparative Analysis
V38_ABSTRACT: Traditional cyber risk assessment methodologies face a critical dilemma: they are either quantitative yet static and context-agnostic (e.g., CVSS), or context-aware yet highly labor-intensive and subjective (e.g., NIST SP 800-30). Consequently, organizations struggle to scale risk assessment to match the pace of evolving threats. This paper presents an automated, context-aware risk assessment framework that leverages the reasoning capabilities of publicly available Large Language Models (LLMs) to operationalize expert knowledge. Rather than positioning the LLM as the final decision-maker, the framework decouples semantic interpretation from risk scoring authority through a transparent, deterministic Dynamic Metric Engine. Unlike complex closed box machine learning models, our approach anchors the AI’s reasoning to this expert-validated metric schema, with weights derived using the Rank Order Centroid (ROC) method from a survey of 101 cybersecurity professionals. We evaluated the framework through a comparative study involving 15 diverse real-world vulnerability scenarios ( $C_{1}-C_{15}$ ) and three supplementary sensitivity stress tests ( $C_{16}-C_{18}$ ). The validation scenarios were independently assessed by a cohort of ten senior human experts and two state-of-the-art LLM agents (GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash). The results show that the LLM-driven agents achieve scoring consistency closely aligned with the human median (Pearson $r$ ranging from 0.9390 to 0.9717, Spearman $\rho $ from 0.8472 to 0.9276) against a highly reliable expert baseline (Cronbach’s $\alpha =0.996$ ), while reducing the assessment cycle time by more than $100\times $ (averaging under 4 seconds per case vs. a human average of 6 minutes). Furthermore, a dedicated context sensitivity analysis ( $C_{13}-C_{15}$ ) indicates that the framework adapts risk scores based on organizational context (e.g., SME vs. Critical Infrastructure) for identical technical vulnerabilities. Importantly, the system is designed not merely to replicate expert intuition, but to enforce bounded, policy-consistent risk evaluation under predefined governance constraints. Overall, these findings suggest that commercially available LLMs, when constrained by expert-validated metric schemas, can support reproducible, transparent, and real-time risk assessments.

V38_RECOVERED_TITLE: Blockchain-Assisted Time-Bound Encrypted Matching for Trustworthy Agentic-AI Edge Networking
V38_ABSTRACT: Agentic edge networking relies on autonomous agents running closed-loop perception–reasoning–planning pipelines to coordinate in real time. A central coordination primitive is to decide whether two exchanged risk descriptors refer to the same event, while preventing privacy leakage and ensuring trustworthy execution under zero-trust, multi-stakeholder participation. Public-key encryption with equality test (PKEET) enables matching over encrypted values, yet existing designs are poorly suited to agentic edge deployments because they often assume a designated tester or trusted authority, provide coarse delegation that amplifies token-leakage damage, and lack decentralized accountability against dishonest or selective execution. We propose Blockchain-assisted Time-Bound PKEET (BT-PKEET) that offers secure multi-agent coordination with decentralized trust and provenance. BT-PKEET binds encryption and authorization to short time windows via PRF-derived window keys, and supports three least-privilege token types (ciphertext-bound, peer-bound, and event-bound) to constrain inference abuse and collusion surfaces in low-entropy descriptor spaces. We further develop a contract-friendly, unified on-chain verification equation that supports arbitrary token combinations and records audit-ready provenance for accountability. To enable continuous tracking without costly re-encryption or re-authorization, we introduce bridge tokens that incrementally refresh cross-window capability, with fast revocation by halting bridge publication. Experiments on a Hyperledger Fabric prototype show stable on-/off-chain Test overhead (7×–11×) and reduced window migration cost (1.7×–2.0×), achieving order-of-magnitude gains over pairing-heavy baselines while providing consortium-wide auditable coordination outcomes.

V38_RECOVERED_TITLE: Agentic AI in Distributed SDN: Synchronization and Design Framework
V38_ABSTRACT: Large-scale Software-Defined Networking (SDN) deployments are increasingly adopting Physically Distributed but Logically Centralized (PDLC) control planes, in which multiple controllers must coordinate to maintain a consistent global view of the network. In practice, this creates a persistent trade-off between state consistency and synchronization overhead under limited control-plane budgets. Existing AI-based synchronization solutions often rely on centralized learning and decision components, which can reduce scalability and introduce single-point-of-failure-like dependence. This paper presents a design framework for adaptive synchronization in PDLC SDN from an agentic AI perspective. The objective is to express synchronization as a budget-aware decision process that can be learned by controller-resident agents while enabling cooperative learning without centralized run-time action selection. We model synchronization as a budget-aware Markov Decision Process (MDP) with explicit state, action, and reward definitions that capture staleness, constrained neighbor selection, and benefit-cost tradeoffs. Based on this formulation, we adopt Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (CTDE): decentralized Actors make local synchronization decisions at run time, while a trainingtime Critic provides coordination signals to stabilize multi-agent learning. The framework is instantiated with Communication Multi-Agent Actor-Critic (C-MAAC) and extended with an Attention-Based Critic (ABC-MAAC), where attention suppresses low-impact inter-controller relations and emphasizes influential ones before value estimation. Complexity verification shows linear per-update scaling for C-MAAC and an additional quadratic interaction term for ABC-MAAC due to pairwise attention, while preserving decentralized, budget-aware run-time execution.

V38_RECOVERED_TITLE: Prompt Injection Through Operational Data Feeds: A Structural Governance Gap in OT-Connected Agentic AI Systems
V38_ABSTRACT: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in smart grid and smart city operational technology (OT) environments, ingesting live SCADA feeds, historian logs, and event streams to construct operational context and execute actions through tool-use interfaces. This paper identifies and characterizes a control-layer failure mode arising from the intersection of false data injection and agentic decision-making: prompt injection through live operational data feeds. Existing industrial control system (ICS) security standards—including NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, ISA/IEC 62443, and NERC CIP—enforce data integrity and system behavior but do not explicitly enforce trust validation at the point where ingested data becomes agentic decision context. Actuation gatekeeping enforces authority boundaries at command execution; it does not govern what context the agent ingests upstream. An adversary who compromises a SCADA feed or historian stream manipulates the operational picture presented to a human approver. The approver authorizes. The gate executes correctly. The attack has already succeeded. This paper makes three contributions: (1) it characterizes OT feed injection as a control-layer failure mode unaddressed by MITRE ATLAS, NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, ISA/IEC 62443, or NERC CIP at the agentic decision context level—these frameworks were built for deterministic control systems and passive data consumers, not for agents that transform ingested data into decision authority; (2) it validates the attack path through scenario-driven evaluation against the AAIGF-E governance framework, confirming that actuation gatekeeping leaves the upstream data layer unprotected; and (3) it defines a control-layer extension requiring source attestation and content plausibility validation at OT feed ingestion points, upstream of the approval gate. Formalization constraints and specific directions for MITRE ATLAS and ISA/IEC 62443 working groups are documented.

The fairness pipeline iteratively refines fairness through a systematic cycle where current metrics are automatically evaluated, specific issues diagnosed, appropriate mitigation techniques selected and improvements verified until fairness thresholds are reached or diminishing returns observed while carefully balancing fairness gains against performance impact. When tested on four benchmark datasets, the framework showed noticeable improvements in fairness metrics. Notably, the Adult dataset demonstrated a 75% mean fairness improvement across all evaluated metrics. The real strength of this framework lies in its flexibility as it adjusts bias mitigation depending on the dataset and the type of bias it detects. Although challenges exist, including increased computational requirements, this approach demonstrated significant effectiveness in identifying and mitigating bias during experimental evaluations.
